ig_caption:
Blitz 900, rapid 1200? Nothing is wrong with you.

Chess.com and Lichess keep a separate rating for each speed, and each one only moves when you play that speed. Fast games test quick pattern-spotting; slower games reward careful thinking, so many players are stronger at one than another. Each rating also compares you only with people who play that speed, so the numbers were never meant to match.

The simple fix: pick the one speed you most want to improve and judge your progress there. Play the others for fun.

slides.title: Each speed has its own rating
slides.body: Chess.com and Lichess keep a separate rating for each speed, such as bullet, blitz and rapid. Each one only moves when you play that speed.
slides.note: So your numbers can drift far apart without anything being wrong.

slides.title: Fast chess tests other skills
slides.body: In bullet, quick hands and spotting familiar patterns matter most. In rapid you have time to think ahead, so careful calculation pays off.
slides.note: Lots of players are clearly stronger at one speed than another.

slides.title: Different speeds, different crowds
slides.body: Each rating only compares you with people who play that speed on that site. The bullet crowd and the rapid crowd are not the same group.
slides.note: Comparing your blitz with a friend's rapid tells you very little.

slides.title: Pick one to judge
slides.body: Choose the speed you most want to improve and track your progress there. Slower games give you time to think and to spot your own mistakes.
slides.note: Play the faster ones for fun, and don't worry about their dips.

slides.title: Blitz, rapid or bullet,
slides.sub: Your whole rating history, on one print.
